◆Contents

DogSense HUD is Symbolic Synapse's real-time canine behaviour display for Rokid glasses. It combines a dog's posture and movement with its vocalisations, and shows the result on the monochrome-green HUD. The system reports what it measured and which rule fired. It does not claim to translate what a dog is thinking.

2Purpose and design principle

Dogs communicate mainly through kinematics (posture, tail-wag asymmetry, ear carriage, weight distribution) together with acoustics (pitch, inter-bark interval, harmonic-to-noise ratio). Neither channel is enough alone. A high-pitched bark can mean play solicitation or barrier frustration, depending on the body posture that goes with it.

DogSense pairs the glasses' camera and microphone with a local GPU server. It extracts both channels, fuses them with explicit rules, and projects behavioural telemetry onto the wearer's HUD in real time.

Design principle. The HUD shows measurements and the rule that fired, such as "Stiff + forward + low growl", together with a behavioural state. Every state can be traced back to observable cues. The network outputs are evidence for the rules, not the final verdict.

Throughout the build, three rules from the original concept were treated as requirements:

  • Never interpret sound alone. Audio is always read alongside posture, and a play bow overrides a growl.
  • Compare against this dog, not a universal threshold. Ear and posture cues are scored as deviations from a per-dog baseline.
  • Make urgency readable without colour. The waveguide is monochrome green, so urgency is carried by geometry and line weight.

3System architecture

Heavy vision and audio models would hit the glasses' thermal and battery limits within minutes. The workload is therefore split: the glasses capture and display, and a local GPU server on the same Wi-Fi does all the inference.

Rokid glasses · Android app

Camera: CameraX, 720p, JPEG at ≤ 15 fps
Microphone: AudioRecord, 16 kHz mono PCM, 100 ms chunks, unprocessed source
Gravity sensor: head roll for ego-motion compensation
SpeechGate: on-device "reverse VAD" that flags the wearer's own voice
HudView: Canvas, black = transparent; reticle, gauges and caption

Body-frame normalisation: cancels camera translation, roll and distance

Neuro-symbolic fusion: ordered rules plus neural priors → state, alert, arousal, valence
Optional VLM: local Ollama model tags the scene trigger every ~3 s

4Visual kinematics

4.1 Pose estimation

The base model is Ultralytics YOLO26n-pose, fine-tuned for 60 epochs on the Ultralytics Dog-Pose dataset (6,773 training and 1,703 validation images, 24 keypoints per dog). The keypoints cover paws, knees, elbows, tail base and tip, ear bases and tips, nose, chin, eyes, withers and throat.

Horizontal-flip augmentation is used with an explicit flip_idx map, so a flipped image keeps correct left and right labels.

Second stage. The pose model misses many dogs that are facing the camera or partly hidden behind bars or fences. A general COCO detector (YOLO26s, "dog" class) therefore runs alongside it. Any dog it finds that the pose model missed is re-read by the pose model on a padded, zoomed crop. If no skeleton comes back, the dog still counts as seen and the HUD reports sound only for it.

4.2 Ego-motion compensation

The camera moves with the wearer's head, so screen coordinates cannot reveal subtle movements. Each skeleton is re-expressed in the dog's own body frame:

  • Head roll from the gravity sensor is removed first.
  • The origin is the spine midpoint, the x-axis runs from tail base to withers, and the unit is one spine length. This cancels translation, roll and distance.
  • A second, gravity-aligned copy keeps spine pitch, so a play bow stays measurable.
  • When the spine is hidden or foreshortened (head-on view), the frame falls back to the visible skeleton's centroid and extent.

4.3 Temporal features (30-frame sliding window)

SignalHow it is measured
Tail wagTail-vector angle against the spine. Frequency from zero crossings, amplitude from spread. The left/right bias is reported only in rear or front views, mirrored for front views so that "right" is always the dog's right. Right bias is associated with approach and left bias with withdrawal (Quaranta et al., 2007).
Play bowElbows and withers dropped below the hindquarters relative to gravity, scored against this dog's baseline
Weight shiftSpine midpoint position between rear and front paws. Computed only in lateral views where "forward" is defined.
Ear carriageEar-tip vector projected onto the head axis (nose minus ear base): forward, neutral or pinned
Ear flickLargest ear-carriage change within 200 ms
StiffnessLow skeletal motion energy combined with a still tail

A dilated 1D-CNN (TemporalPoseNet) reads the same 30-frame window: 48 normalised coordinates plus 10 engineered features per frame. It outputs probabilities over six classes: relaxed, play bow, alert, defensive/stiff, anxious and excited.

4.4 Breed morphology

The system does not run a separate breed classifier. Instead, the first ~45 neutral frames of each dog set its baseline ear carriage, front/rear height and tail set. They also classify its morphology as prick, semi or drop ears and full, docked or curled tail. A French Bulldog's ears or a Greyhound's low tail then do not read as alert or fearful. The baselines reset after the dog has been out of view for about a second.

5Bioacoustic analysis

5.1 Front end

  • Wind: a fourth-order 150 Hz high-pass filter, kept running across chunks, plus an adaptive noise-floor estimate.
  • Event detection: energy above 4 × the noise floor, with short gaps bridged. The noise floor is the 20th percentile of 10 ms frame energy over the last 2 s, so detection is the same for any chunk size. An event that reaches the end of a chunk is held until it finishes, so long whines are not split into fake rapid barks.
  • Wearer's voice and other people: every event passes a sound-source gate. The Audio Spectrogram Transformer fine-tuned on AudioSet classifies a 1.5 s window centred on the event, and events it scores as speech, shouting or whistling rather than dog are rejected. An ambiguous event within 0.8 s of confirmed speech counts as part of the same run. Two lighter checks still apply: chunks with speech_prob > 0.6 from the glasses are dropped, and long, moderately harmonic events in the adult speech range (85–255 Hz) are rejected. Sound readings arrive about 0.75 s after the sound, while the gate's window fills.

5.2 Acoustic metrics per event

MetricMethod
Fundamental frequency (F0)Normalised-autocorrelation peak with parabolic interpolation over voiced 64 ms frames. An octave guard takes the shortest period within 10 % of the best correlation, so the tracker does not lock onto a multiple of the true period. Atonal events (HNR < 3 dB) use the spectral peak instead, because F0 is undefined for a growl.
Harmonics-to-noise ratioBoersma (1993) autocorrelation method, median over 40 ms frames, so pitch glides do not smear it
Inter-bark interval and burst rateEvent onsets over a 4 s window
BandsPitch: low < 300 Hz, mid, high > 600 Hz. Tonality: harsh < 3 dB, mixed, tonal > 9 dB.

5.3 Call type

Call type is decided in two ways and combined:

  • Acoustic rules (motivation-structural):
    • Low F0 with low harmonicity reads as a growl or warning.
    • High F0 with high tonality reads as a whine.
    • Rapid mid-range bursts read as play or excitement.
  • VocalCNN: a 4-block CNN on 64-band log-mel spectrograms of 1 s clips, with six classes: none, growl, alert bark, play bark, whine and howl.

The network's label is used only when its confidence is above 0.6. Otherwise the acoustic rules decide.

6Neuro-symbolic fusion

Pure neural classification invents intent when signals conflict. DogSense resolves conflicts with an ordered, deterministic rule base, and the first rule that matches wins:

#ConditionHUD stateAlert
1Play bow > 0.5 and not a threat posture. Overrides any growl.Play Solicitationno
2Stiff > 0.7, weight forward, and the scene trigger is a toy, food or other resourceResource Guardingyes
3Stiff, weight forward, and a growl (or low-pitched bark)Defensive Warningyes
4Stiff and weight forward, no soundHigh Arousal / Fixatedyes
5Ears pinned and weight back, or left-biased wag, or a whine with tense postureAnxious / Appeasingno
6Whine with a loose bodySeeking / Distress Callno
7Wag > 1.5 Hz, loose body, not left-biasedFriendly / Excitedno
8Bark, or ears forward with moderate stiffnessAlert / Vigilantno
9Dog tracked, nothing else firesRelaxedno

The two example rules from the concept are implemented directly:

Play bow (Δy elbows ≫ Δy hips) ∧ growl (low F0)            ⟹  Play Solicitation (safe)
Stiff tail (ω_wag ≈ 0) ∧ forward weight ∧ low F0, harsh     ⟹  Defensive Warning (alert)

Continuous gauges. Each rule carries a (valence, arousal) target. This target is blended with the pose network's class priors (weight 0.25) and the audio class prior (weight 0.15); the audio weight is dropped when a play bow overrides a growl. The result is boosted by burst rate and ear flicks and smoothed with an exponential moving average (α = 0.35) for a calm display.

Scene context. If a local vision-language model is running in Ollama (for example qwen2.5vl:7b), a downsampled frame is tagged every ~3 s, off the critical path. Example tags are Approaching Stranger, Other Dog, Resource/Toy and Leash Tension. The tag feeds rule 2 and shows as "TRIGGER:" on the HUD. If no VLM is reachable, it backs off for a minute.

7The monochrome HUD

The Rokid waveguide shows a single green channel, and black is see-through. A red-versus-green alert is impossible, so urgency is shown through form:

  • Target reticle: four corner brackets around the dog, so the dog itself stays visible. During an alert the brackets thicken from 3 to 6 px and blink at about 3 Hz.
  • Arousal gauge: AROUSAL [||||||....] 65%, from calm to hyper-stimulated.
  • Valence gauge: VALENCE [- - - | + + +], from defensive/distressed to playful/relaxed.
  • Caption block: STATE: Play Solicitation (Bow + play growl) normally. An alert gets a boxed ALERT: Defensive Warning with an action line.
  • Cue line and status: the cues that fired (for example "stiff | weight fwd | growl 180Hz"), the morphology calibration state and the round-trip latency.
  • Debug skeleton: the 24-point skeleton overlay. Toggle it with the temple touchpad or the browser checkbox.

8Models and training results

All models were trained locally on the RTX 3090. Weights are in models/.

ModelTraining dataResult (held-out data)File
Dog pose (YOLO26n-pose), 60 epochsDog-Pose, real imagesBox mAP50 0.991 · pose mAP50 0.936 · pose mAP50-95 0.509dog_pose.pt, .onnx (12.9 MB)
TemporalPoseNet, 40 epochs30,000 synthetic sequences98.6 % accuracy on synthetic datatemporal_pose.pt
VocalCNN, 30 epochs12,000 synthetic calls99.8 % accuracy on synthetic datavocal_cnn.pt
The temporal and vocal results do not measure real-world accuracy. No public dataset pairs behaviour labels with Dog-Pose keypoint sequences. The dog-audio datasets (DMAD, CREMD) need manual download and licence acceptance. Both heads were therefore pre-trained on procedural data, passed through the same featuriser as live data with random viewpoint, head motion, scale, occlusion and breed morphology. Their scores only show that the networks learned the designed signatures. This is why the rule base, not the networks, makes the decision.

8.1 Synthetic data generators (training/synth.py)

  • Kinematics: a side-view canonical skeleton deformed per behaviour, varying tail lift, wag frequency, amplitude and bias, bow depth, lean, ear angle, jitter and bounce. It is then rendered with breed variation (ear type, tail length including docked, leg length) and camera effects (yaw foreshortening, drift, zoom, roll, detector noise, dropped keypoints).
  • Audio: harmonic-stack calls with set F0 ranges, glides, harmonicity and growl amplitude modulation, mixed with wind rumble, hiss and speech-like hum.

8.2 Fine-tuning on real data

python training/train_temporal.py --videos data/clips --init models/temporal_pose.pt
#   data/clips/<relaxed|play_bow|alert|defensive_stiff|anxious|excited>/*.mp4
python training/train_audio.py --data data/audio --init models/vocal_cnn.pt
#   data/audio/<none|growl|bark_alert|bark_play|whine|howl>/*.wav

9Running the system

9.1 Server

pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m server.app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8765      # add --vlm qwen2.5vl:7b if Ollama is running

GET /health reports the device and which models loaded. Measured round trip on the RTX 3090 over localhost: 37.8 ms median, 82.7 ms p90 per frame.

9.2 Browser HUD (no glasses needed)

Open http://localhost:8765/. Choose Start webcam + mic or Open video file, and tick skeleton for the keypoint overlay. The page uses the same wire protocol as the glasses and draws the same HUD. It processes live and saves nothing.

9.3 Desktop simulator (saves video)

python tools/simulate.py --video my_dog.mp4 --wav my_dog.wav --skeleton --out hud_output.mp4

For best results, film 10–30 s of the dog at eye height, side-on, with the whole dog in frame and sound on. Allow about 3 s for calibration.

9.4 Glasses app

cd android
./gradlew assembleDebug -PserverUrl=ws://<PC LAN IP>:8765/ws
adb install app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk

Behind a TLS-inspecting proxy, set GRADLE_OPTS=-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStoreType=Windows-ROOT. Python uses the truststore package for the same reason.

11Verification

CheckResult
Unit tests (pytest tests), including the sound-only labelling rule and the sound-source gate (human runs rejected, dog calls kept): body-frame invariance to rotation, scale and shift; kinematic signatures per behaviour; play bow overrides growl; stiff + forward + growl gives a warning; resource trigger gives guarding; F0 and HNR accuracy; growl and whine pitch bands through the streaming analyser9 / 9 pass

Defects found and fixed during verification:

  • Long vocalisations were split at 100 ms chunk boundaries and read as rapid barks.
  • Per-chunk spectral gating removed sustained calls. The streaming path now uses a running high-pass filter.
  • Growl pitch was unstable. It now uses the spectral peak.
  • Head-on views failed body-frame normalisation. A centroid fallback was added.
  • Weight shift was reported in views where it is meaningless. It is now gated to lateral views.
  • A dog that was visible but still warming up was labelled "not in view".

Section 12 lists four further defects found with real glasses footage, all fixed in this version.

12Field test with Rokid glasses footage

The first real-world test used a 61-second clip filmed through Rokid glasses on 22 October 2026. The clip shows two dogs in a garden, with barking and whining. It was processed offline by the desktop simulator, which runs the same pipeline and models as the live server.

ItemDetail
Source2400 × 1800 H.264 at 30 fps, rotated 90°, with AAC audio. Converted to 960 × 1280 upright video and 16 kHz mono audio.
Commandsimulate.py --video dog.mp4 --wav dog.wav --skeleton --out … --log telemetry.jsonl
Processing time1,830 frames in about 100 s on the RTX 3090 (offline, every frame processed)
OutputsDogSense_HUD_test.mp4 (HUD video with original sound) and data/test/telemetry.jsonl (per-frame readings)

12.1 What the system reported

TimeMain HUD stateCues measured
6–7 s, 12 s, 30–45 sAlert / VigilantAlert-type barks at about 270–490 Hz, and higher calls
24–37 s, 48 sSeeking / Distress CallTonal whines at about 1,200–1,600 Hz
9 s, 15 s, 54 sRelaxedTail wag 1.5–3 Hz, ears forward or pinned
51 sFriendly / ExcitedWagging with barking
Whole clipNo alertsNo stiff, forward-weighted posture with a growl was seen

A dog was first tracked in 522 of 1,830 frames (28 %). After the two-stage detector was added (section 12.3), the same clip was re-processed and a dog was tracked in 1,031 of 1,830 frames (56 %). For much of the clip the camera points at the garden, gate or plants, so the remaining "No dog" frames are mostly correct. The labels have not yet been checked against a person's judgement of what the dogs were doing.

DefectCauseFix

All 7 unit tests still pass after the fixes, and the clip was re-processed to confirm them: the bow and stale-state false readings are gone.

In IMG_2390 the dogs were shown as "Alert / Vigilant" (ears forward, alert barks at about 425–1,300 Hz) while barking at the gate, and as "Relaxed" between barks. No alerts fired. These readings have not yet been checked against a person's judgement.

12.4 The wearer's own voice

Reviewing the first clip, the wearer pointed out that the loud "hey, hey, hey" at about 5 s was them telling the dogs to stop. The HUD had reported it as alert barking. The existing filters missed it: each "hey" was short, loud and harmonic, so it did not match the "long speech" rule, and it was as loud as the barks of a nearby dog.

A pretrained Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AudioSet, 527 sound classes) was tested on the clip's loudest events. It scored the three "hey"s, a whistle at 34.7 s and several later sounds as human speech or whistling, and the 7.8 s bark as dog. Several "dog sounds" in the first test were therefore the wearer.

Finding while building the gateFix
AST verdicts on short (0.6 s) snippets were unstable; the same "hey" scored human or dog depending on the framingWindow lengths of 0.6, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 s were compared on ten labelled events. A 1.5 s centred window made no wrong calls; the two "hey"s it was unsure of are caught by the speech-run rule.
Live-sized audio chunks (33 ms) finalised events with almost no surrounding audio, so the gate could not judge themEvents wait until their full 1.5 s window has arrived, then are cut from the rolling buffer.
Event detection gave different results for 33 ms and 100 ms chunks (14 vs 31 events)The noise floor is now estimated from the last 2 s of audio. Both chunk sizes now give the same results on all three clips.
A synthetic whine measured at 200 Hz instead of about 1 kHz (sub-harmonic error), which put it in the speech rangeOctave guard in the pitch tracker (section 5.2)
Result after the fixesDetail
First clip, 5–7 s ("hey, hey, hey")No bark cues; the HUD reads the dogs' posture (Relaxed / Friendly)
First clip, 30–36 s (whistle and speech)No longer reported as whining or barking
Human sounds rejected per clipFirst clip 44 · IMG_2389 2 · IMG_2390 4. The real barks are kept, for example 7.8 s in the first clip and the off-screen barking in IMG_2389.

This correction came from the person wearing the glasses, who knew what had actually happened. It shows why the next step is labelling the clips against what really happened.

13Limitations and open issues

  • Behaviour and audio heads are synthetic-only. Real-world accuracy is unknown until they are fine-tuned on labelled clips.
  • Pose quality varies by view. Pose mAP50-95 is 0.51. In some head-on images the withers, eyes and tail are missed, which weakens posture cues.
  • Tail asymmetry is only reliable in rear or front views. Side views report frequency and amplitude only.
  • Voice filtering depends on a general-purpose classifier. The AST gate was checked against the wearer's voice and the dogs in three clips. It is not trained on this wearer, these dogs or the glasses' microphone, and short ambiguous sounds can still slip through. The Rokid SDK's own VAD score should be wired in where the firmware exposes it. Sound direction (bursts from the lower visual field) is not yet used.
  • Rokid integration assumes Android-capable glasses. Models that stream through the phone-side SDK need their frames and PCM routed into DogSenseClient.
  • Single dog. Tracking follows one dog (largest first, then highest overlap with its previous box). Barks cannot yet be attributed to a particular dog when two are present.
  • Detector errors in the field. In the first field test the detector missed two dogs in clear view and once boxed a tree. The second-stage detector recovers many misses (section 12.3), but fine-tuning on Rokid footage, including gates and fences, is still needed.
  • Head-on views. Play bow, weight shift and tail-wag direction need a side or rear view, so for dogs facing the wearer the HUD relies more on ears and sound.
  • Latency is measured on localhost. Wi-Fi adds transport delay, and the timestamp comparison assumes the device and server clocks are synchronised.
  • The system describes behaviour; it is not a substitute for a qualified trainer or behaviourist.

14Next steps

  • Label the field test. Mark what the dogs were actually doing in the 61-second clip, and compare it with telemetry.jsonl to get a first real accuracy figure.
  • Collect real footage. Film 10–30 s side-on clips with sound and label them into the six behaviour classes. Then fine-tune temporal_pose.pt and vocal_cnn.pt and measure accuracy on a held-out set of different dogs.
  • Test on hardware. Install on the Rokid glasses, measure Wi-Fi latency and HUD legibility outdoors, and wire in the SDK VAD.
  • Improve pose. Train longer or use a larger pose model, and add head-on and rear-view examples from real walks.
  • Turn on scene context. Pull a VLM into Ollama and evaluate trigger-tag accuracy.
  • Optional. Move pose inference on-device using the exported ONNX model, add recording to the browser HUD, and support multi-dog tracking.
